questions.stem: A study surveys 1,500 adults about pet ownership and stress. Among cat owners the average stress score is 2.5; among non-owners it is 3.0. Which statement is an INFERENTIAL claim?

options.a: In our sample, cat owners reported 20% lower stress than non-cat owners.
options.b: Cat ownership is associated with a 20% reduction in stress among all adults.
options.c: The sample contained 1,500 adults.
options.d: The mean stress of cat owners was 2.5.
options.e: The box plot of stress scores had two groups.

questions.explanation: Descriptive statements stay inside the sample we observed. The inferential statement generalises to the broader adult population, which is the whole point of moving from the sample to the population.

questions.stem: Which of the following are examples of INFERENTIAL statistics rather than descriptive statistics?

options.a: Computing the median income of the survey respondents.
options.b: Performing a hypothesis test comparing a sample mean to a known population mean.
options.c: Creating a box plot of test scores.
options.d: Estimating the population proportion using sample data.
options.e: Computing the standard deviation of a sample.

questions.explanation: Inferential statistics generalise from a sample to a population: hypothesis testing (b) and estimating a population proportion (d). The others only summarise the data at hand.

questions.stem: The lecture notes that uncertainty in a conclusion can come from several places. Which of the following are listed as sources of uncertainty?

options.a: An incorrect sampling strategy.
options.b: An incorrect measurement of stress.
options.c: A small sample size.
options.d: The use of decimals in the dataset.
options.e: Choosing to report a median instead of a mode.

questions.explanation: The three sources named are an incorrect sampling strategy, incorrect measurement, and small sample size. Cosmetic reporting choices do not themselves create uncertainty about the population.

questions.stem: In the 1936 Literary Digest poll, 2.4 million people were surveyed and Landon was predicted to win with 57% of the vote. Roosevelt actually won with 62%. According to the lecture, why did such a large poll fail?

options.a: The sample size was too small to be reliable.
options.b: The magazine polled its subscribers and car owners, who during the Great Depression were mostly wealthy Republicans.
options.c: The poll was conducted before the election was decided.
options.d: The responses were counted incorrectly by the magazine.
options.e: The poll used a random sampling method, which is unsuitable for elections.

questions.explanation: The poll was enormous but biased: it surveyed the magazine's own subscribers and car owners, who were disproportionately wealthy Republicans. The lesson the lecture draws is explicit: a large sample size does not fix a biased sampling strategy.

questions.stem: Which statement about sample size and sampling bias is true?

options.a: A large sample size can compensate for a biased sampling strategy.
options.b: A large sample size guarantees the sample is representative.
options.c: A large sample size reduces random error but does not fix a biased sampling strategy.
options.d: Sample size is irrelevant whenever probability sampling is used.
options.e: Bias can only occur when the sample is smaller than the population.

questions.explanation: Sample size reduces random error, i.e. sampling variability. It cannot repair a systematically unrepresentative sampling frame. The Literary Digest poll is the lecture's example of exactly this.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to say something about elderly women living in Sweden but ends up sampling only women living in elderly care facilities. Which statement is correct?

options.a: The target population and the sampled population are different groups.
options.b: The sampled population is a subset of the sample.
options.c: The sample is the full group the researcher wants to generalise to.
options.d: The observation unit is the elderly care facility.
options.e: Target and sampled populations are identical unless the sample is random.

questions.explanation: The target population is everyone you want to say something about (elderly women in Sweden); the sampled population is the group you could actually reach (those in care facilities). They are ideally the same but often are not, because some individuals are unreachable.

questions.stem: Which of the following are TRUE statements about study design terminology?

options.a: The observation unit is the unit you actually study.
options.b: In the CSS programme the observation unit is most often the individual.
options.c: The sampled population is always larger than the sample.
options.d: A sample is the full group you want to make claims about.
options.e: The target population and the sampled population may differ when some individuals are unreachable.

questions.explanation: The observation unit is what you study (usually individuals); target and sampled populations can diverge because some people are unreachable; and the sample is by definition a subset of the sampled population, so it is smaller, not larger. A sample is never the full target group.

questions.stem: A Ph.D. student draws a lottery among ALL Ph.D. students at LiU and randomly selects 10. Which statement is correct?

options.a: The target population is not equal to the sampled population here.
options.b: This is a random sample because each student has an equal chance of selection.
options.c: This introduces sampling bias because 10 is a small number.
options.d: The observation unit is the department rather than the student.
options.e: This is a convenience sample because the student chose the number 10.

questions.explanation: A lottery over the complete list is random sampling, and the target and sampled populations coincide. Small n causes imprecision, not bias. Choosing n = 10 in advance is not what makes a sample a convenience sample.

questions.stem: A Ph.D. student is asked to recruit respondents for a study of how long a Ph.D. at LiU takes, and chooses their friends and department colleagues. Which statement is correct?

options.a: The target population equals the sampled population in this design.
options.b: This is a random sample because the student chose the participants personally.
options.c: The target population is not equal to the sampled population, and sampling bias has been introduced.
options.d: The only problem is the small sample size, not who was selected.
options.e: The observation unit becomes the department rather than the individual.

questions.explanation: Picking your own friends and colleagues produces a non-representative sample and breaks the link between the sampled population and the target population. Bias in sampling leads to incorrect conclusions about the population.

questions.stem: Consider the following R code. What is the value of `a` after the code runs?

options.c: Hello
options.d: World
options.e: The code produces an error, because a is a reserved word.

questions.explanation: R evaluates the right-hand side and stores the result. `a <- 2 + 2` stores 4 in a, so printing `a` gives 4.

questions.stem: Consider the following R code. What is printed?

options.a: Hello
options.b: World
options.c: Hello World
options.d: An error, because a is overwritten
options.e: Nothing, because assignment does not print

questions.explanation: The second assignment replaces the contents of `a`. Assignment overwrites without warning, so the object ends up holding "World".

questions.stem: Consider the following R code. What is printed?

options.e: An error, because a and b are numbers not vectors

questions.explanation: `d * 2` recycles the scalar 2 across the vector, giving 2 4 6 8, while `a + b` is arithmetic on two single stored values, 4 + 6 = 10.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about R data types are TRUE?

options.a: `x <- 2L` creates an integer, because the L suffix forces integer type.
options.b: `x <- 3.14` creates a numeric value.
options.c: `x <- "hello"` creates a character vector.
options.d: `x <- TRUE` creates a logical vector.
options.e: `x <- 2L` creates a numeric value, because integers are a subset of numerics.

questions.explanation: The L suffix explicitly forces integer type, so (e) is false even though R will happily do arithmetic with integers. All of (a) to (d) are true.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about R data structures are TRUE?

options.a: A vector is a one-dimensional list of elements of the same data type.
options.b: A matrix is a two-dimensional list of elements of the same data type.
options.c: A data frame is a two-dimensional list of vectors that may have different types.
options.d: A list may contain elements of different types.
options.e: A data frame can only contain numeric columns.

questions.explanation: A vector is a one-dimensional list of elements of the same data type. A matrix is a two-dimensional list of elements of the same data type. A data frame is a two-dimensional list of vectors that may have different types. A list may contain elements of different types. Only (e) is false.

questions.stem: Consider the output below from R. Which statements are true?

options.a: The output is a data.frame with two elements.
options.b: The first element is a character vector.
options.c: The second element is a character vector.
options.d: The output is a matrix with two rows.
options.e: The output is a list with two elements.

questions.explanation: The [[1]] / [[2]] indexing is the signature of a list, and the elements have different types, which is exactly what distinguishes a list from a matrix or a data frame column set. The first element 1 2 3 is numeric, not character.

questions.stem: You want a factor with the levels in the order Low, Medium, High. Which R code is correct?

options.a: factor(x, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))
options.b: factor(x) - it always sorts alphabetically, which is what we want
options.c: levels(x) = c("Low", "Medium", "High")
options.d: as.character(x) <- c("Low", "Medium", "High")
options.e: sort(x, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))

questions.explanation: You set the level order by passing `levels` to `factor()`. Bare `factor(x)` takes the levels in alphabetical order, which would give High, Low, Medium.

questions.stem: Consider the following R code. What does `f(3)` return?

options.d: An error, because f is not a built-in function
options.e: The function definition itself

questions.explanation: The assignment stores a function in `f`, so calling it applies `x^2` to the argument. Note that the right-hand side is evaluated before the assignment, so `f` exists as a function object only after that line runs.

questions.stem: For a study of the relationship between neighbourhood characteristics and well-being, a team selects 10 municipalities, then 5 urban districts within each, then 50 adults aged 20-64 per district from the national population register. 2,150 people respond. Identify the target population, the sampled population, the sample and the observation unit.
questions.answer: Target population: all Swedish adults aged 20-64 about whom the team wants to make claims. Sampled population: the adults aged 20-64 listed in the Swedish population register, i.e. the group actually sampled from. Sample: the 2,150 individuals who responded. Observation unit: the individual adult, since each respondent contributes one survey record.

rubric.text: Target population identified as all Swedish adults aged 20-64
Sampled population identified as the register-based group that could actually be drawn from
Sample identified as the 2,150 responders
Observation unit identified as the individual person

questions.stem: Explain the difference between a vector, a matrix, a data frame and a list in R.
questions.answer: A vector is a one-dimensional sequence of elements that all share one data type, and is created with c(). A matrix is a two-dimensional version of the same idea, so all its elements still share one type. A data frame is also two-dimensional, but its columns are separate vectors that may have different types. A list is a multidimensional collection whose elements may have different types, which is why it is the most flexible of the four.

rubric.text: Vector described as 1-dimensional, single type, made with c()
Matrix described as 2-dimensional, still single type
Data frame described as 2-dimensional columns that may differ in type
List described as a collection whose elements may differ in type

questions.stem: R has six data types but the course covers four. Name them and give one example value for each.
questions.answer: The four covered types are numeric (for example 3.14), integer (for example 3 or 2L), logical (TRUE, FALSE, or NA) and character (for example "SDS1"). The two types deliberately left out are complex and raw, which students rarely or never use.

rubric.text: Numeric and integer both named
Logical and character both named
Complex and raw correctly identified as the excluded types

questions.stem: Explain what happens to the text that follows a hash symbol (#) in an R script, and why you would use it.
questions.answer: Anything after the hash symbol is ignored by R and is never run, so it is treated as a comment. Comments are used to annotate code so that a reader, including your future self, can follow the logic of a script.

rubric.text: Text after # is ignored / not executed
Purpose given as documenting or annotating code

questions.stem: Explain why the following R code does not modify the original object `x`, and describe what `<-` does when it is used on an object that already exists.
questions.answer: The right-hand side is evaluated first and only then is the result assigned to the name on the left, so the original value of x is not touched until the assignment completes. When the name already exists, `<-` simply overwrites the previous contents without warning, which is why reusing a name like `a` for a different kind of object can cause confusion later.

rubric.text: Right-hand side evaluated first, then assigned
`<-` overwrites an existing object without warning

questions.stem: Write the R code that creates a vector containing the values 1, 2, 3, 4, and then doubles every element of it. No need to give the final printed result.
questions.answer:
```r
d <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
d * 2
```
The scalar 2 is recycled across the vector, giving 2 4 6 8.

rubric.text: Vector created with c(1, 2, 3, 4)
Doubling performed by multiplying the vector by 2

questions.stem: A factor is stored internally as integers with labels attached. Explain what this means in practice, and why it matters when you want a specific order of categories.
questions.answer: Because a factor is stored as integers with a set of labels attached, the numeric codes are not meaningful in themselves; what matters is the mapping to labels and the order of the levels. The order of levels controls both sorting and plotting, so a factor used as a plotting variable will be drawn in the order of its levels rather than alphabetically, which is why the level order must often be set explicitly.

rubric.text: Explanation that storage is integer codes plus a label mapping
Levels control ordering, so order must sometimes be set explicitly

questions.stem: Explain, using the Literary Digest poll as an example, why a very large sample does not guarantee a correct conclusion.
questions.answer: A large sample reduces random error but it cannot repair a biased sampling strategy, because a systematically unrepresentative frame is not fixed by collecting more of the same units. The Literary Digest polled 2.4 million people but only its own subscribers and car owners, who during the Great Depression were mostly wealthy Republicans, so it predicted Landon at 57% while Roosevelt won with 62%.

rubric.text: Large sample reduces random error but not bias
Literary Digest mechanism described: subscribers and car owners
Correct consequence given: wrong prediction despite huge n

questions.stem: Which of the following variables are CATEGORICAL rather than numerical?

options.a: Number of siblings
options.b: Educational level
options.c: Height in cm
options.d: Whether a person owns a car
options.e: Age in years

questions.explanation: Educational level and car ownership name categories rather than measuring a quantity. Siblings, height and age all take numeric values that can be meaningfully compared and averaged.

questions.stem: You count 1 'yes' and 3 'no' in a sample. What does `prop.table(table(x))` return?

options.a: The counts 1 and 3
options.b: The proportions 0.25 and 0.75
options.c: The percentages 1 and 3
options.d: The counts divided by the number of columns
options.e: A cumulative distribution

questions.explanation: `table()` gives counts; `prop.table()` converts them to proportions that sum to 1, so here 1/4 = 0.25 and 3/4 = 0.75.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a contingency table?

options.a: To summarise the mean of a numeric variable
options.b: To display the counts of two categorical variables crossed against each other
options.c: To compute the variance of a sample
options.d: To plot two continuous variables
options.e: To store the levels of a factor in a specific order

questions.explanation: A contingency table crosses two categorical variables so you can see how their counts co-occur. In R you build one with a two-argument table(), e.g. `table(x$class, x$survived)`.

questions.stem: Consider the following R code and its output. What does the call do?

options.a: It computes row proportions for each group
options.b: It computes column proportions for each group
options.c: It computes overall proportions for each group
options.d: It computes the difference in proportions between groups
options.e: It computes a chi-squared statistic

questions.explanation: `prop.table(x, margin = 1)` normalises each row so it sums to 1, giving the proportions within each group. margin = 2 would instead normalise columns.

questions.stem: Which plot is the natural choice for summarising a single categorical variable?

options.a: A histogram
options.b: A bar plot
options.c: A scatterplot
options.d: A density plot
options.e: A box plot

questions.explanation: Bar plots compare counts or proportions across discrete categories. Histograms, density plots, scatterplots and box plots are all for numerical data.

questions.stem: In a grouped bar plot of two categorical variables, what does `fill =` most naturally encode?

options.a: The variable whose categories become the different bar colours
options.b: The size of the bars
options.c: The statistical significance of the comparison
options.d: The order of the x-axis
options.e: The missing values in the data

questions.explanation: You map one variable to `aes(x = ...)` for the axis and another to `fill = ...` so the categories of the second variable become the bar colours.
questions.code:
ggplot(titanic_data, aes(x = class, fill = survived)) +
  geom_bar()

questions.stem: Consider `calc_percent <- function(x, total) (x / total) * 100`. Which statements about calling it are TRUE?

options.a: `calc_percent(25, 100)` passes arguments by position
options.b: `calc_percent(total = 100, x = 25)` passes arguments by name
options.c: The arguments must always be given in the order they are defined
options.d: `calc_percent(25)` works because `x` defaults to 25
options.e: The function returns 25 in both of the first two calls

questions.explanation: R allows arguments to be passed positionally or by name, so the first two are both valid and give the same result of 25. Order is not forced, and `x` has no default, so the fourth claim is false.

questions.stem: Consider `calc_percent_default <- function(x, total = 100) (x / total) * 100`. What does `calc_percent_default(25)` return?

options.a: An error, because `total` is missing
options.e: NA

questions.explanation: `total = 100` is a default, so it fills in automatically: 25/100 * 100 = 25.

questions.stem: What is the difference between the two lines below?

options.a: `install.packages("ggplot2")` downloads and installs the package; `library(ggplot2)` attaches it for use in the current session.
options.b: They are exact synonyms for each other.
options.c: `install.packages()` attaches the package; `library()` installs it.
options.d: `library()` can only be run once per year.
options.e: Neither line is needed if ggplot2 is already installed.

questions.explanation: Installation puts the package on disk so it persists; library() merely makes it available in the session you are working in, and must be run again in each new session.

questions.stem: Which of the following are TRUE statements about subsetting?

options.a: `df$age` accesses the single column `age`
options.b: `df[1, ]` returns the first row
options.c: `df[, 3]` returns the third column
options.d: `df[, 3]` returns the third row
options.e: `df[4:9, 2]` returns rows 4 to 9 of column 2

questions.explanation: The first index is the row and the second is the column, so `[, 3]` is a column, not a row. Only (d) is false.

questions.stem: Which of the following commands return EXACTLY the value `3`?
questions.explanation: `[2]` returns the single element 3. `[3]` also returns 3 but that is not among the options here, the logical selection returns TWO elements (3 and 3), `== 3` returns a logical vector, and `[-1]` drops the first element.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of the pipe `|>` as described in the lecture?

options.a: It makes R run faster
options.b: It lets you chain operations, passing the result forward, for more readable code
options.c: It automatically removes missing values
options.d: It is required in order to load a package
options.e: It converts a vector into a data.frame

questions.explanation: The pipe takes the value on its left and passes it as the first argument of the function on its right, which removes deeply nested parentheses and reads more like a sequence of steps. It does not change speed, missing values, or data types.

questions.stem: You want to keep only rows where `class == "3rd"`. Which is the idiomatic dplyr way?

options.a: `select(titanic_data, class == "3rd")`
options.b: `titanic_data |> filter(class == "3rd")`
options.c: `titanic_data |> arrange(class == "3rd")`
options.d: `titanic_data |> summarise(class == "3rd")`
options.e: `titanic_data |> mutate(class == "3rd")`

questions.explanation: filter() keeps or drops ROWS. select() chooses columns, arrange() sorts rows, summarise() collapses the data, and mutate() adds or changes columns.

questions.stem: Which statements about these verbs are TRUE?

options.a: `select()` picks out columns
options.b: `mutate()` adds or modifies columns
options.c: `arrange()` sorts rows
options.d: `arrange(desc(fare))` sorts from largest to smallest
options.e: `arrange(desc(fare))` sorts from smallest to largest

questions.explanation: `desc()` requests descending order, so (d) is right and (e) is wrong. A bare `arrange(fare)` would sort ascending.

questions.stem: Consider the following code. What does it return?

options.a: One mean fare for the whole dataset
options.b: One mean fare per class, plus a grouped object
options.c: One mean fare per class, ungrouped, in one row
options.d: A new column on every row
options.e: A contingency table of class by survival

questions.explanation: `group_by(class) |> summarize(...) |> ungroup()` produces one row per class AND leaves the result grouped, because `ungroup()` is applied afterwards. Dropping the trailing `ungroup()` gives the ungrouped one-row-per-class answer.
questions.code:
titanic_data |>
  group_by(class) |>
  summarize(mean_fare = mean(fare, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()

questions.stem: What is the difference between `.by = class` inside `mutate()` and using `group_by(class)` first?

options.a: `.by` only works inside summarise(), never mutate()
options.b: `.by` performs the grouping for that one call without leaving the result grouped
options.c: `group_by()` is faster than `.by`
options.d: `.by` ignores missing values
options.e: There is no difference; they are exactly the same

questions.explanation: `.by` groups only for the duration of that call and returns an ungrouped object, which avoids the extra ungroup() step and the risk of forgetting it.
questions.code:
titanic_data |>
  mutate(mean_fare = mean(fare, na.rm = TRUE), .by = class)

questions.topic: Getting a sense of the data
questions.stem: Which statements about these functions are TRUE?

options.a: `str()` summarises the structure of a data.frame, showing column types
options.b: `summary()` gives distributional summaries such as mean and median
options.c: `dim()` returns the number of rows and columns
options.d: `str()` returns the arithmetic mean of a column
options.e: `dim()` returns the column names

questions.explanation: `str()` shows structure rather than statistics, so (d) is false. `dim()` gives the two dimensions, and the column names come from `names()` or `colnames()`.

questions.stem: A bar plot of a factor with levels High school, Bachelor, Master, PhD puts the categories in alphabetical order by default, which puts Bachelor first. What is the fix?

options.a: Rename the categories so they happen to sort in the intended order
options.b: Set the order of the levels explicitly with `factor(levels = ...)`
options.c: Use `arrange()` on the plotting data
options.d: Convert the factor to character
options.e: Use `mutate()` to rename each value

questions.explanation: ggplot2 sorts a factor by its level order, not alphabetically, so setting the levels explicitly is the direct fix. The lecture makes this point about the education variable.

questions.stem: Which R code sorts `titanic_data` by fare from largest to smallest?

options.a: `arrange(titanic_data, fare)`
options.b: `titanic_data[order(titanic_data$fare, decreasing = TRUE), ]`
options.c: `titanic_data[order(titanic_data$fare), ]`
options.d: `select(titanic_data, order(fare))`
options.e: `sort(titanic_data$fare)`

questions.explanation: `order()` returns the positions that would put the values in order, and `decreasing = TRUE` reverses it. Using the result as a row index returns the sorted rows. A bare `sort()` returns only the sorted fares, losing every other column.

questions.stem: Consider the vector `x <- c("a", "b", "a", NA)`. What does `table(x)` return?

options.a: Counts a = 1, b = 1, and NA = 1
options.b: Counts a = 2, b = 1, and does not include NA by default
options.c: Counts a = 2, b = 1, and includes NA = 1
options.d: Returns the proportions directly
options.e: Returns an error because of the missing value

questions.explanation: `table()` ignores missing values unless you ask for them with `useNA = "ifany"`. So a = 2 and b = 1, and the NA is silently dropped.

questions.stem: Which statements about graphs are TRUE?

options.a: A graph's title states what is being shown
options.b: The x-axis and y-axis name the variables and their units
options.c: A legend explains what colours or shapes mean
options.d: A graph should never include a source note
options.e: Axis labels should be omitted when the variable names are obvious

questions.explanation: Title, labelled axes with units, and a legend are the standard elements the lecture lists. Citing the source is good practice rather than something to omit, so (d) is false; and omitting axis labels is never right.

questions.stem: Write the R code that counts how many observations fall in each of the `class` categories of `titanic_data`, and then converts those counts to proportions. No need to give the numerical output.
questions.answer:
```r
table(titanic_data$class) |>
  prop.table()
```
`table()` produces the counts and `prop.table()` divides them by the total so they sum to 1.

rubric.text: `table()` used to get the counts
`prop.table()` applied to convert to proportions

questions.stem: Write the R code that produces a two-way table of `class` by `survived`, and then shows the proportion within each class.
questions.answer:
```r
table(titanic_data$class, titanic_data$survived) |>
  prop.table(margin = 1)
```
A two-argument `table()` builds the contingency table, and `margin = 1` normalises within each row so each class sums to 1.

rubric.text: Two-argument `table()` used to cross the two variables
`prop.table(margin = 1)` used for within-class proportions

questions.stem: Write the R code that computes the mean fare for each passenger class using dplyr.
questions.answer:
```r
titanic_data |>
  group_by(class) |>
  summarize(mean_fare = mean(fare, na.rm = TRUE))
```
`group_by()` splits the data by class, `summarize()` computes the mean within each group, and `na.rm = TRUE` drops missing fares.

rubric.text: `group_by(class)` used to split by class
`summarize()` with `mean(fare, na.rm = TRUE)` used for the mean
Pipe used to chain the steps

questions.code:
titanic_data |>
  group_by(class) |>
  summarize(mean_fare = mean(fare, na.rm = TRUE))

questions.stem: Explain what the pipe operator `|>` does, and why it was introduced in R 4.1.0 rather than being available from the start.
questions.answer: The pipe takes the value on its left and passes it as the first argument of the function on its right, so a chain of operations can be written as a sequence of steps instead of deeply nested parentheses. It was added natively in R 4.1.0 in 2021; before that the magrittr package supplied `%>%`, which meant base R itself could not offer the operator without depending on a package.

rubric.text: Describes passing the left value as the first argument of the right call
Mentions readability / avoiding nested calls
Notes R 4.1.0 (2021) and the magrittr `%>%` predecessor

questions.stem: Explain the difference between passing an argument by position and passing it by name, and mention how a default value is set.
questions.answer: Positional matching assigns arguments in the order they appear in the function definition, so the first value goes to the first parameter. Named matching writes `name = value` and is safer because it stays correct if the definition order changes. A default is set by putting the value after an equals sign in the definition, as in `function(x, total = 100)`, and is used automatically when the argument is omitted.

rubric.text: Position explained as order-based assignment
Name explained as explicit `name = value`
Default explained as `arg = value` in the definition

questions.stem: Give three different ways to select rows of `titanic_data` where `class == "3rd"` and `survived == "yes"`, and say which dplyr verb is the one the course prefers.
questions.answer: One way is base R logical indexing, `titanic_data[titanic_data$class == "3rd" & titanic_data$survived == "yes", ]`. A second is the dedicated function, `subset(titanic_data, class =="3rd" & survived == "yes")`. The third, and the one the course prefers, is the pipe with the dplyr verb: `titanic_data |> dplyr::filter(class == "3rd" & survived == "yes")`.

rubric.text: Base R logical indexing given
`subset()` given
`dplyr::filter()` given and identified as preferred

questions.stem: Write the R code for a grouped bar plot showing the count of passengers in each class, split by whether they survived.
questions.answer:

questions.stem: Drawing a red card and drawing a black card from a single draw. How are these events related?

options.b: Disjoint, because they cannot happen at the same time
options.c: Independent, because colour is unrelated to the draw
options.d: Complementary, because they cover the sample space
options.e: Equally likely

questions.explanation: They are disjoint (mutually exclusive) since one card cannot be both red and black, so the probability of the intersection is 0. They are not complementary, because they do not cover the whole sample space - there are also face cards that are neither.

questions.stem: Why is P(red or black) = 26/52 + 26/52 = 1 for a shuffled deck?

options.b: Because the two events are complementary: they are disjoint and together cover the whole sample space
options.c: Because every card has probability 1
options.d: Because red and black are joint events

questions.explanation: Red and black are disjoint and their union is the entire deck, so they are complements. For disjoint events the addition rule reduces to simple addition, which is why the probabilities sum to exactly 1.

questions.stem: What is the general addition rule for any two events A and B?

options.a: P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B)
options.b: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)
options.c: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
options.d: P(A) = P(A or B) - P(B)
options.e: P(A or B) = 1 - P(A and B)

questions.explanation: The subtraction of the intersection is required whenever A and B are not disjoint, because the overlapping cases would otherwise be counted twice. For disjoint events the intersection is 0 and the rule collapses to (c).
