questions.stem: Which statements about parameters and statistics are TRUE?

options.a: A parameter describes a population characteristic.
options.b: A statistic is calculated from a sample.
options.c: A parameter changes from sample to sample.
options.d: The population mean is written mu and the sample mean with an x-bar.
options.e: A statistic is fixed once the population is defined.

questions.explanation: Parameters are fixed population quantities while statistics vary with the sample, so (c) and (e) are both wrong. The lecture's summary line is that parameters are what we want to know and statistics are what we can compute.

questions.stem: Match each term to the correct example for estimating the mean height of all Norrkoping residents. Which statement is TRUE?

options.a: The estimand is 169.03 cm
options.b: The estimator is the sample mean formula
options.c: The estimate is mu
options.d: The estimand and the estimate are the same thing
options.e: The estimator is a fixed number, not a formula

questions.explanation: The estimand is the unknown population quantity mu, the estimator is the rule or formula used (here the sample mean), and the estimate is the particular number obtained from one sample, such as 169.03 cm.

questions.stem: Which statements about an estimator are TRUE?

options.a: An estimator is a function of the data.
options.b: An estimator is a random variable.
options.c: An estimator is a single fixed number once defined.
options.d: The sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean.
options.e: An estimator maps the sample space onto numerical values.

questions.explanation: An estimator is a rule rather than a number, and precisely because it maps the sample space onto values it is itself a random variable. That is what (c) gets wrong.

questions.stem: The sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean. What does "unbiased" mean?

options.a: The sample mean always equals the population mean
options.b: On average the sample mean hits the true population mean, i.e. E[Xbar] = mu
options.c: The sample mean has zero variance
options.d: The sample mean is normally distributed
options.e: The sample mean is always smaller than the population mean

questions.explanation: Unbiasedness is a statement about expectation, not about any single sample: the sample mean can be above or below mu in a given sample, but its expected value equals mu. The variance is sigma squared over n, which is not zero.

questions.stem: What happens to the variance of the sample mean as the sample size n increases?

options.a: It increases
options.b: It decreases, because Var(Xbar) = sigma^2 / n
options.c: It stays constant
options.d: It becomes equal to sigma^2
options.e: It becomes zero for any n

questions.explanation: The variance of the sample mean is sigma squared over n, so larger samples give a more precise estimate. It approaches zero but only reaches it in the limit, so (e) is false.

questions.stem: What does the law of large numbers state?

options.a: As n grows, the sample mean converges to the population mean
options.b: As n grows, the sample variance becomes exactly zero
options.c: The sample mean is normally distributed for large n
options.d: The population is normally distributed
options.e: The median always equals the mean for large n

questions.explanation: The LLN says the sample mean gets arbitrarily close to the population mean as n grows. Making the sample mean approximately normal is the central limit theorem, which is a separate and stronger claim, so (c) is not the LLN.

questions.stem: What does the central limit theorem state?

options.a: The sample mean converges to the population mean as n grows
options.b: For large n the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal, whatever the shape of the population
options.c: The population must be normally distributed for inference to work
options.d: The standard deviation of the sample equals the population standard deviation
options.e: The sample size must exceed the population size

questions.explanation: The CLT is what makes z-based inference possible without knowing the population shape: the sample mean is approximately normal for large n even when the population itself is not. Approximate convergence of the mean is the LLN, so (a) is not the CLT.

questions.stem: A distribution is strongly right-skewed. Which statement is TRUE?

options.a: The mean is smaller than the median.
options.b: The mean is larger than the median.
options.c: The mean and median are always equal for a symmetric distribution.
options.d: The median is more affected by outliers than the mean.
options.e: The mode cannot be identified for a skewed distribution.

questions.explanation: A long right tail pulls the mean upward, so the mean exceeds the median. The median is the more robust of the two, which is why the last two options have it backwards.

questions.stem: For a study estimating the average height of all Norrkoping residents, state the estimand, the estimator and the estimate.
questions.answer: The estimand is the population mean height mu of all Norrkoping residents. The estimator is the rule used to compute it from data, namely the sample mean formula Xbar = (1/n) sum of X_i. The estimate is the particular number obtained by applying that formula to one sample, for example 169.03 cm from n = 50.

rubric.text: Estimand correctly identified as the unknown population mean mu
Estimator correctly identified as the sample mean formula
Estimate correctly identified as the observed value from one sample

questions.stem: Explain what the central limit theorem states and why it matters for inference.
questions.answer: The CLT states that for large n the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal even when the population itself is not normally distributed. It matters because it lets us use the normal machinery, z-scores and confidence intervals, to make inferences about the population without ever needing to know the population's shape, which is rarely known in practice.

rubric.text: States the approximate normality of the sampling distribution of the mean
Notes it holds regardless of the population shape
Explains it enables normal-based inference without knowing the population

questions.stem: Write down the formula for the variance of the sample mean, and explain what happens to it as n increases.
questions.answer: `Var(Xbar_n) = (1/n^2) * sum of Var(X_i) = (n sigma^2) / n^2 = sigma^2 / n`, using the independence of the observations. As n increases the variance shrinks, so the sample mean becomes a more precise estimate of the population mean; it approaches zero but only reaches it in the limit.

rubric.text: Variance of sample mean given as sigma squared over n
Derivation or intermediate term involving n sigma squared over n squared shown
Explains that larger n gives a more precise estimate

questions.stem: Explain the difference between a probability mass function, a probability density function and a cumulative distribution function, and say which applies to a fair die.
questions.answer: A PMF gives the probability of each individual outcome and applies to discrete variables, so for a fair die it is 1/6 at each face. A PDF describes the relative likelihood across a continuous range and does not itself integrate to a probability at a point. A CDF gives P(X <= x) and is a step function for a discrete variable like a die, but a smooth increasing curve for a continuous one.

rubric.text: PMF defined as the probability of each discrete outcome
PDF defined as relative likelihood for a continuous variable
CDF defined as P(X <= x) and distinguished as step versus smooth
Correctly states the PMF applies to a fair die with value 1/6

questions.stem: Shampoo bottles have a nominal fill of 36 mL with a standard deviation of 0.11. Without calculating, write down the R code for the probability that a bottle contains less than 35.8 mL.
questions.answer:
```r
pnorm(35.8, mean = 36, sd = 0.11)
```
`pnorm()` returns P(X <= x) for a normal variable, so this is the area under the PDF to the left of 35.8. The value is about 0.0345, which the lecture slide rounds to 0.0344.

rubric.text: `pnorm()` used as the correct function
Mean and standard deviation supplied as named arguments
States that this is P(X <= 35.8), the area to the left

questions.stem: Explain the law of large numbers and how it differs from the central limit theorem.
questions.answer: The law of large numbers says that as the sample size grows the sample mean converges to the population mean, so it is a statement about where the sample mean ends up. The central limit theorem additionally says that for large n the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal, which is a statement about its shape. The CLT builds on the LLN and is what justifies normal-based inference.

rubric.text: LLN stated as convergence of the sample mean to the population mean
CLT stated as approximate normality of the sampling distribution
Relationship between the two explained

questions.stem: For each situation, name the distribution you would expect to model it and give the reason: the number of heads in 20 coin tosses, the number of customers arriving in an hour, and the height of a randomly chosen adult.
questions.answer: Heads in 20 tosses is binomial, because it counts successes across a fixed number of independent trials with two outcomes. Customers in an hour is Poisson, because it counts events in a fixed interval. Adult height is normal, because it is a natural measurement that is roughly symmetric and bell-shaped.

rubric.text: Binomial correctly matched to coin tosses with a reason
Poisson correctly matched to arrivals per interval with a reason
Normal correctly matched to height with a reason

questions.stem: Explain what it means to say the sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean, and why small samples are still a problem even when the estimator is unbiased.
questions.answer: Unbiased means the expected value of the sample mean equals the population mean, E[Xbar] = mu, so the estimator is on target in the long run even though any single sample can fall above or below mu. Small samples remain a problem because bias is only about the average: for small n the variance sigma squared over n is still large, so individual sample means fluctuate widely around mu.

rubric.text: Unbiasedness explained via E[Xbar] = mu
Notes that a single sample may still deviate from mu
Explains that large variance at small n causes wide fluctuation

questions.stem: What are the steps of a hypothesis test as laid out in the lecture?

options.a: Compute the p-value, then reject H0, then state the hypotheses
options.b: Formulate H0, compute the test statistic, calculate the p-value, draw conclusions
options.c: Collect data, then choose the test, then report
options.d: Compute a confidence interval, then reject H0, then conclude
options.e: State Ha, compute the standard error, then stop

questions.explanation: The four steps are: formulate the null hypothesis, compute the test statistic which measures how far the estimate sits from what H0 predicts, compute the p-value of a statistic at least as extreme under H0, and then draw the conclusion.

questions.stem: What is the general formula for the test statistic?

options.a: test statistic = point estimate / null value
options.b: test statistic = (point estimate - null value) / standard error of the estimate
options.c: test statistic = point estimate - null value
options.d: test statistic = standard error / point estimate
options.e: test statistic = (null value - point estimate) / standard error

questions.explanation: The test statistic measures how many standard errors the estimate lies from the null value, so it is the difference divided by the standard error. Reversing the numerator, as in option (e), only flips the sign and breaks the usual right-tail convention.

questions.stem: The population mean is 170 cm, the sample mean is 179 cm and the standard error is 1.83. What is the z-score, and what does it mean?

options.a: z is about 0.05, so the sample mean is very close to the population mean
options.b: z is about 4.9, so the sample mean is about 4.9 standard errors above the population mean
options.c: z is about 1.96, so the result is significant at 5%
options.d: z is about 4.9, so the sample mean is 4.9 cm above the population mean
options.e: z cannot be computed without knowing the standard deviation

questions.explanation: z = (179 - 170)/1.83 is about 4.9. Because the statistic is in units of standard errors rather than centimetres, the number describes how many SE away the value sits, not a distance in cm.

questions.stem: Consider the R code below. What does it return?
questions.explanation: `lower.tail = FALSE` returns the upper-tail area beyond the value, which is the p-value here, about 4.37e-07. The value 0.9655 is the lower tail and 0.0345 belongs to the bottle example from Lecture 5.

questions.stem: The p-value of a test is about 4.4e-07. What is the correct interpretation?

options.a: There is a 4.4e-07 probability that the null hypothesis is true.
options.b: If the null hypothesis were true, the probability of a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one is about 4.4e-07.
options.c: There is a 4.4e-07 probability that the result is a fluke.
options.d: The null hypothesis has been proven false with certainty.
options.e: 4.4e-07 of the sample data are outliers.

questions.explanation: The p-value is always conditional on H0 being true and describes the observed or more extreme statistic. It is not the probability that H0 is true, and it never proves anything with certainty.

questions.stem: What is the definition of bias for an estimator?

options.a: Bias(theta-hat) = E[theta-hat] + theta
options.b: Bias(theta-hat) = E[theta-hat] - theta
options.c: Bias(theta-hat) = theta - E[theta-hat] / n
options.d: Bias(theta-hat) = Var(theta-hat)
options.e: Bias(theta-hat) = p-value

questions.explanation: Bias is the expected value of the estimator minus the true parameter, so an unbiased estimator has Bias = 0. Note that option (c) has the opposite sign, which would just be a negated bias.

questions.stem: Which statements are TRUE?

options.a: Sampling bias is a type of missing data problem.
options.b: Attrition means individuals drop out of a longitudinal study.
options.c: Item non-response means individuals skip certain questions in a survey.
options.d: Missing data reduces the effective sample size, which increases the standard error.
options.e: Missing data can introduce bias only if it is random.

questions.explanation: It is missing data that is NOT random that can introduce bias and invalidate inference, which is the opposite of what (e) claims.

questions.stem: What critical value do you use for a 95% confidence interval for a mean with a large sample?
questions.explanation: The two-sided 95% critical value is the 97.5th percentile of the standard normal, 1.96. A common trap is 1.645, which is the 95th percentile and therefore the critical value for a 90% interval, not 95%.

questions.stem: Which statements about confidence intervals are TRUE?

options.a: A confidence interval is an interval estimate of plausible values for the population parameter.
options.b: About 95% of the sample means would fall inside a given 95% CI.
options.c: About 95% of the data points would fall inside a given 95% CI.
options.d: Increasing the confidence level from 95% to 99% makes the interval wider.
options.e: A single 95% CI lets you be certain the true parameter is inside it.

questions.explanation: The 95% refers to how often intervals computed across many samples cover the true parameter, not to the data or the sampling distribution, so (b) and (c) are both wrong. And a single interval still contains uncertainty, so (e) is wrong.

questions.stem: Why does increasing the confidence level produce a wider interval?

options.a: A higher confidence level requires a smaller critical value
options.b: A higher confidence level requires a larger critical value, and the interval half-width is critical value times standard error
options.c: A higher confidence level reduces the standard error
options.d: A higher confidence level increases alpha
options.e: A higher confidence level shrinks the sample size

questions.explanation: The interval is point estimate plus or minus critical value times standard error, and a higher confidence level needs a larger critical value while the standard error is unchanged. This is the trade-off the lecture notes: a wider interval is more likely to contain the parameter but less informative.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval computed from a population with mean 170 is (172.06, 177.94). Which statement is TRUE?

options.a: The population mean is 175
options.b: The standard error of the sample mean is 1.5
options.c: The sample mean is 175
options.d: 95% of the population falls inside this interval
options.e: The interval must contain the true mean because it is a 95% interval

questions.explanation: The half-width 2.94 equals 1.96 times the standard error, so the standard error is about 1.5. A confidence interval is an interval for the population parameter, not for the population values or the sample mean, and even then it is not a certainty.

questions.stem: Which of the following are TRUE statements about the t-distribution functions in R?

options.a: `dt()` gives the probability density function
options.b: `pt()` gives the cumulative distribution function
options.c: `qt()` gives quantiles
options.d: `rt()` generates random samples
options.e: `pt()` can only be used for a normal distribution

questions.explanation: The four functions mirror the normal set d/p/q/r but for the t distribution, and the fifth option is wrong because `pt()` is the t-distribution CDF, not the normal one. The lecture lists exactly these four.

questions.stem: The population mean height is 170 cm and the standard error of the sample mean is 1.83 cm. A sample of 30 gives a mean of 179 cm. Without calculating, write down the formula you would use for the test statistic.
questions.answer: `z = (xbar - mu) / SE = (179 - 170) / 1.83`, which is a z-score of about 4.9, meaning the observed sample mean sits roughly 4.9 standard errors above the hypothesised population mean.

rubric.text: Test statistic written as (xbar - mu)/SE
Values 179, 170 and 1.83 correctly substituted
States the interpretation in standard error units

questions.stem: Describe the four steps of a hypothesis test, and state the conclusion when the resulting p-value is approximately 0.
questions.answer: First formulate the null hypothesis, for example that the sample comes from a population with mean 170. Second compute the test statistic, which measures how far the observed estimate is from the null value in units of standard error. Third compute the p-value, the probability of a statistic at least as extreme as the observed one under H0. Fourth draw the conclusion: with p approximately 0 the result is so unlikely under H0 that we reject it and conclude the sample probably comes from a population with a different mean.

rubric.text: Hypothesis formulation given as step 1
Test statistic explained as distance in SE units
P-value defined as an H0-conditional tail probability
Conclusion of rejecting H0 correctly stated

questions.stem: Without doing calculations, write down the formula for the 95% confidence interval for a population mean, and state the formula for any confidence level.
questions.answer: For any confidence level the interval is point estimate plus or minus critical value times standard error. For 95% with a large sample this is `(xbar - 1.96 * s/sqrt(n), xbar + 1.96 * s/sqrt(n))`. Ideally sigma is used rather than s, but when the population standard deviation is unknown s is used provided n is large enough, say greater than 30.

rubric.text: General form given as estimate plus or minus critical value times SE
95% critical value 1.96 correctly used
Standard error written as s/sqrt(n)
Notes sigma is preferred but s is used when unknown and n is large

questions.stem: Define bias in terms of the estimator and the true parameter, and explain how sampling bias would affect a height study.
questions.answer: Bias is the expected value of the estimator minus the true parameter, Bias(theta-hat) = E[theta-hat] - theta, and an estimator is unbiased when that is zero. In a height study, if we unknowingly sampled mainly members of a basketball club, the expected sample mean would be shifted upward relative to the true population mean, giving a positive bias and a wrong conclusion about the population.

rubric.text: Bias defined as E[estimator] minus the true parameter
Unbiased estimator correctly identified as having bias of zero
Basketball club example used to illustrate upward bias of the mean

questions.stem: Name two ways missing data can arise besides sampling bias, and explain the consequence of missing data for a hypothesis test.
questions.answer: Two further sources are attrition, where individuals drop out of a longitudinal study, and item non-response, where individuals skip particular questions in a survey. Missing data reduces the effective sample size, which increases the standard error and therefore reduces the power of the test, and when the missing data is not random it can additionally introduce bias and invalidate the inference.

rubric.text: Attrition and item non-response both named
Reduced sample size linked to a larger standard error
Reduced power correctly identified as the consequence
Non-random missing data linked to bias and invalid inference

questions.stem: Explain what a 95% confidence interval does and does not tell you, and why it is described as a random interval.
questions.answer: A 95% CI is an interval estimate of plausible values for the population parameter: across many samples, about 95% of the intervals computed this way would contain the true parameter. It does not say that 95% of sample means or 95% of the data points fall inside it. It is called random because its endpoints move from sample to sample as the sample mean and standard error change, which is why no single interval can be certain.

rubric.text: Describes the repeated-samples coverage meaning of 95%
Explicitly rules out the claim about sample means or data points
Explains randomness via sample mean and SE changing between samples

questions.stem: Explain what a p-value is and state one thing it is NOT.
questions.answer: A p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one actually obtained. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it does not measure the size or importance of an effect, only how inconsistent the data are with the null.

rubric.text: P-value defined as an H0-conditional tail probability
States that it is NOT the probability that H0 is true
Notes it says nothing about effect size or importance

questions.stem: Write the R code to compute the p-value for an observed sample mean of 179 when the hypothesised mean is 170 and the standard error is 1.83, for an upper-tailed test.
questions.answer:
```r
pnorm(179, mean = 170, sd = 1.83, lower.tail = FALSE)
```
Setting `lower.tail = FALSE` returns the upper-tail probability, which is the p-value for an upper-tailed test, about 4.37e-07. The equivalent forms `1 - pnorm(179, 170, 1.83)` and standardising to a z-score give the same answer.

rubric.text: `pnorm()` used with the observed value as the first argument
`lower.tail = FALSE` used to obtain the upper tail
Mean 170 and sd 1.83 correctly supplied

questions.stem: How do one-sided and two-sided tests differ?

options.a: A one-sided test has rejection regions in both tails; a two-sided test has only one.
options.b: A two-sided test has rejection regions in both tails; a one-sided test has the rejection region in only one tail.
options.c: They differ only in the sample size required.
options.d: A one-sided test always uses the t-distribution; a two-sided test uses the normal.
options.e: They produce identical critical values for the same alpha.

questions.explanation: The alternative hypothesis decides the shape: mu != mu0 needs both tails, while mu > mu0 or mu < mu0 needs one. Consequently the critical values and p-values differ between the two, so (e) is false.

questions.stem: A manufacturer claims light bulbs last at least 1000 hours on average. A sample of 20 bulbs gives a mean of 975 and a standard deviation of 50. Which test is appropriate?

options.a: Two-sided, H0: mu = 1000 versus Ha: mu != 1000
options.b: One-sided, H0: mu <= 1000 versus Ha: mu > 1000
options.c: One-sided, H0: mu >= 1000 versus Ha: mu < 1000
options.d: Two-sided, H0: mu = 975 versus Ha: mu = 1000
options.e: A chi-squared test, since two values are involved

questions.explanation: The claim to be challenged is that the mean is at least 1000, so the null sets mu >= 1000 and the alternative is that the mean is lower. The observed 975 is below the claimed value, confirming the direction.

questions.topic: Type I and Type II errors
questions.stem: What is a Type I error?

options.a: Failing to reject H0 when it is false
options.b: Rejecting H0 when it is true
options.c: Rejecting Ha when it is true
options.d: Using the wrong critical value
options.e: Choosing a one-sided test instead of a two-sided one

questions.explanation: A Type I error is a false positive: rejecting a null hypothesis that is actually true. Its probability is the significance level alpha. Failing to reject a false null is the Type II error.

questions.topic: Type I and Type II errors
questions.stem: Which statements are TRUE?

options.a: The significance level alpha is the probability of making a Type I error.
options.b: Beta is the probability of a Type II error.
options.c: The power of a test is 1 - beta.
options.d: Power is the probability of correctly rejecting H0 when it is false.
options.e: Reducing alpha always reduces beta, so power improves.

questions.explanation: There is a trade-off: tightening alpha to reduce false positives typically makes it harder to reject, which raises beta and lowers power. So the final statement has the relationship backwards.

questions.stem: For a two-sided test at alpha = 0.05, within which values of the test statistic do you FAIL to reject H0?
questions.explanation: The rejection regions are the two tails beyond plus or minus 1.96, so the acceptance region is the interval from -1.96 to 1.96. Using 1.645 would be the region for a 90% two-sided interval, not 95%.

questions.stem: The 95% CI computed for a sample mean is (172.06, 177.94). You test H0: mu = 175 at the 5% significance level. What is the conclusion, given the observed sample mean is 173.0?

options.a: Reject H0, because 173.0 is below the interval
options.b: Fail to reject H0, because 173.0 lies inside the acceptance region
options.c: Reject H0, because 175 lies inside the interval
options.d: Fail to reject H0, because 175 lies inside the interval
options.e: The test cannot be performed without the standard error

questions.explanation: For a two-sided test at alpha = 0.05 you fail to reject exactly when the observed estimate lies inside the corresponding 95% CI. Since 173.0 is between 172.06 and 177.94, H0 is not rejected, and equivalently 175 lies inside the CI.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between a two-sided hypothesis test at significance level alpha and a confidence interval?

options.a: A 95% CI always corresponds to a one-sided test at alpha = 0.05
options.b: Failing to reject H0 at level alpha is equivalent to the (1 - alpha) confidence interval containing the null value
options.c: Rejecting H0 means the null value lies inside the (1 - alpha) CI
options.d: They are unrelated quantities
options.e: A 99% CI corresponds to a test at alpha = 0.01 one-sided

questions.explanation: This duality is the standard link: the null value falls outside the interval exactly when the test rejects at that level. So (b) and its logic are correct, while (c) states the opposite of the truth.

questions.stem: What is the standard error for the difference between two independent sample means?

options.a: SE = s/sqrt(n)
options.b: SE = sqrt(s1^2/n1) + sqrt(s2^2/n2)
options.c: SE = sqrt(s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2)
options.d: SE = (s1 + s2)/n
options.e: SE = sqrt(s1^2 + s2^2)

questions.explanation: The variances of the two independent sample means add, so the standard error is the square root of the sum of s1 squared over n1 and s2 squared over n2. Option (b) incorrectly adds the two standard errors rather than the two variances.

questions.stem: Which statements are TRUE?

options.a: A confidence interval for a proportion is point estimate plus or minus critical value times the standard error of the proportion.
options.b: The standard error of a sample proportion involves sqrt(p-hat times (1 - p-hat) over n).
options.c: The standard error of a difference in proportions adds the two variances under the square root.
options.d: A hypothesis test for a single proportion uses the normal distribution rather than the binomial.
options.e: Proportions can only be used for continuous variables.

questions.explanation: The proportion machinery is built on the normal approximation to the binomial, which is why the SE has the familiar squaring form. All of (a) to (d) hold; (e) is false because proportions are for categorical, binary-type variables.

questions.stem: Consider this R code. What is its purpose?

options.a: To compute the sample proportions directly
options.b: To run a two-sample test for equality of proportions between the two groups
options.c: To compute a confidence interval for a single proportion
options.d: To test whether a die is fair
options.e: To compute a chi-squared test for independence

questions.explanation: `prop.test()` with two sets of successes and totals performs a two-sample test of equal proportions, which is the default alternative, whereas a single vector of successes and totals would test one proportion.

questions.stem: Consider this R code. What is the value of `p1_hat_se`?
questions.explanation: `p1_hat <- 160/200` is 0.8, and the code computes p1_hat * (1 - p1_hat) / 200 = 0.8 * 0.2 / 200 = 0.0008. The quantity being tested is the variance of the proportion, and its square root 0.028 is the standard error itself.

questions.stem: When should a t-test be used rather than a z-test?

options.a: Always, because R has no z-test function
options.b: When the population standard deviation is unknown, so the sample standard deviation is substituted
options.c: Only when the sample size exceeds 30
options.d: Only when testing a proportion
options.e: When the null hypothesis is one-sided

questions.explanation: The z-test requires knowing the population sigma, which is rarely available, so substituting s leads to the t-test and its t-distribution. Neither sample size nor the direction of the alternative decides this.

questions.stem: Consider the code below. What does it compute?

options.a: A one-sided p-value from a z-statistic
options.b: A two-sided p-value for a t-test with 9 degrees of freedom
options.c: A one-sided p-value for a t-test with 2 degrees of freedom
options.d: The critical value for a 95% t interval
options.e: The probability of a t statistic equal to t_stat

questions.explanation: `2 * pt(t_stat, df = 9)` takes the lower tail and doubles it, which is how you get a two-sided p-value from a t statistic, and `df = 9` fixes the degrees of freedom at 9. The normal equivalent would use `pnorm()` instead of `pt()`.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between a one-sided and a two-sided hypothesis test, and state how the confidence level differs between them for a given alpha.
questions.answer: A two-sided test has the alternative mu != mu0, so the rejection region lies in both tails of the distribution, whereas a one-sided test has the alternative mu > mu0 or mu < mu0 and the rejection region in only one tail. For a given alpha, a one-sided test corresponds to a confidence level of 1 - alpha, while a two-sided test corresponds to 1 - alpha/2, so their critical values and p-values differ.

rubric.text: Two-sided described as alternative mu != mu0 with both tails
One-sided described as one direction with a single tail
Correctly gives confidence levels 1 - alpha and 1 - alpha/2
Notes the critical values and p-values therefore differ

questions.topic: Type I and Type II errors
questions.stem: Define a Type I and a Type II error, give the symbol for each, and explain the trade-off between them.
questions.answer: A Type I error, with probability alpha, is rejecting H0 when it is actually true, a false positive. A Type II error, with probability beta, is failing to reject H0 when it is false, a false negative, and the power of the test is 1 - beta. There is a trade-off because tightening alpha to reduce false positives makes rejection harder, which raises beta and lowers power.

rubric.text: Type I defined as rejecting a true H0, symbol alpha
Type II defined as failing to reject a false H0, symbol beta
Power correctly given as 1 - beta
Trade-off between alpha and beta explained

questions.stem: For a two-sided z-test at alpha = 0.05, write down the condition on the test statistic under which you reject H0, and the corresponding condition on the sample mean.
questions.answer: You reject H0 when the statistic falls outside plus or minus 1.96, that is when `(xbar - mu0)/ (s/sqrt(n)) < -1.96` or the same quantity is greater than 1.96. Translating to the sample mean this is `xbar < mu0 - 1.96 * s/sqrt(n)` or `xbar > mu0 + 1.96 * s/sqrt(n)`, so the acceptance region is `mu0 plus or minus 1.96 * s/sqrt(n)`.

rubric.text: Rejection condition on the test statistic given as beyond plus or minus 1.96
Equivalent condition on the sample mean derived
Acceptance region identified as mu0 plus or minus 1.96 times s/sqrt(n)

questions.stem: Explain how a hypothesis test and a confidence interval relate, using an example with a 95% CI of (172.06, 177.94) and a test of H0: mu = 175.
questions.answer: For a two-sided test at significance level alpha, you fail to reject H0 exactly when the corresponding 1 - alpha confidence interval contains the null value, and you reject exactly when it does not. Here the null value 175 lies inside (172.06, 177.94), so at the 5% level we fail to reject H0, which is also what seeing the observed mean of 173.0 inside the acceptance region tells us.

rubric.text: Duality between test at level alpha and the 1 - alpha CI stated
States that rejection happens when the null value is outside the interval
175 correctly identified as lying inside the interval
Conclusion of failing to reject correctly drawn

questions.topic: Working in R for a hypothesis test
questions.stem: Explain how this R output should be read: `t = 2.5, df = 29, p-value = 0.017`, `alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 50`, `95 percent confidence interval: 51.2 58.8`, `mean of x 55`.
questions.answer: This is a one-sample t-test comparing the sample mean to a null value of 50. The alternative is two-sided, that the true mean differs from 50, and the test statistic is 2.5 with 29 degrees of freedom. The p-value of 0.017 is below 0.05, so we reject H0 at the 5% level; equivalently the 95% CI of (51.2, 58.8) excludes 50. The sample mean is 55.

rubric.text: Identifies the test as a one-sample t-test against a null value of 50
States the alternative is two-sided, mean not equal to 50
Reports the test statistic and degrees of freedom
Draws the correct decision at the 5% level from p = 0.017
Links the decision to the CI excluding 50

questions.stem: Two independent groups have sample standard deviations 15 and 20 with sample sizes 100 and 100. Without calculating the final number, write down the formula for the standard error of the difference in means.
questions.answer: `SE(xbar1 - xbar2) = sqrt(s1^2/n1 + s2^2/n2) = sqrt(15^2/100 + 20^2/100)`, obtained by adding the two variances under the square root because the samples are independent. If the samples were paired you would instead work with the differences within pairs.

rubric.text: Formula given as sqrt of the sum of the two variances
Substitutes 15^2/100 and 20^2/100
Notes the independence assumption

questions.stem: Without doing calculations, write down the formula for the standard error of a sample proportion p-hat from a sample of size n.
questions.answer: `SE(p-hat) = sqrt(p-hat * (1 - p-hat) / n)`. It takes the same shape as the standard error of the mean, and a confidence interval is then p-hat plus or minus the critical value times this standard error.

rubric.text: Formula given as sqrt of p-hat(1 - p-hat)/n
Connects it to the CI form estimate plus or minus critical times SE

questions.stem: Explain why a t-test is used when the population standard deviation is unknown, and write the R code for a two-sided one-sample t-test.
questions.answer: A z-test requires the population standard deviation sigma, which is almost never known. Substituting the sample standard deviation s makes the statistic follow a t-distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom rather than a normal one, and the corresponding critical values come from `qt()` rather than `qnorm()`. For two independent samples the code is `t.test(x, y)` and for one sample against a null value it is `t.test(x, mu = 50)`.

rubric.text: Explains the z-test needs the unknown population sigma
States that substituting s gives a t-distribution with n - 1 df
Gives the R code for a two-sided one-sample t-test

questions.stem: Which statements about correlation are TRUE?

options.a: A correlation of 1 indicates a perfect positive linear relationship.
options.b: A correlation of -1 indicates a perfect negative linear relationship.
options.c: A correlation of 0 means the variables are unrelated.
options.d: Correlation is a specific measure of association between two continuous variables.
options.e: Correlation requires the two variables to be categorical.

questions.explanation: A correlation near 0 means no LINEAR relationship only, so it can still hide a strong non-linear pattern, which is why (c) is false. Correlation is defined for two continuous variables, so (e) is false.

questions.stem: Consider this R output: `t = 5.4738, df = 48, p-value = 1.579e-06`, `cor = 0.6199323`. Which statements are TRUE?

options.a: The sample correlation is about 0.62.
options.b: The test rejects H0: rho = 0 at the 5% level.
options.c: There is evidence that income and high-school graduation are positively correlated.
options.d: The 95% confidence interval of about (0.41, 0.77) contains 0.
options.e: The test has 48 degrees of freedom.

questions.explanation: The 95% CI of (0.4128, 0.7661) excludes 0, so the statement that it contains 0 is false. That is also exactly why the test rejects, since a null value outside the interval means rejection at that level.

questions.stem: Under H0 that rho = 0, what is the standard error of the sample correlation r, and how many degrees of freedom does the test statistic have?

options.a: SE(r) = sqrt((1 - r^2)/(n - 2)) with n - 2 degrees of freedom
options.b: SE(r) = sqrt(r^2/(n - 1)) with n - 1 degrees of freedom
options.c: SE(r) = (1 - r^2)/n with n degrees of freedom
options.d: SE(r) = sqrt((1 - r^2)/(n - 1)) with n - 1 degrees of freedom
options.e: SE(r) = r/sqrt(n) with n degrees of freedom

questions.explanation: The standard error of r is sqrt((1 - r squared)/(n - 2)) and the statistic follows a t distribution with n - 2 degrees of freedom, because r is built from two estimated means rather than one. The lecture also notes this standard error is only valid when rho = 0.

questions.stem: Which statements about Spearman's correlation are TRUE?

options.a: It is the Pearson correlation computed on the ranks of the variables.
options.b: It measures monotonic association rather than only linear association.
options.c: It is robust to outliers.
options.d: It is obtained in R with `cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman")`.
options.e: It cannot detect a relationship where larger states are richer but not linearly.

questions.explanation: Spearman's coefficient is specifically designed to capture monotonic patterns that Pearson misses, which is the whole point of the Alaska example where Pearson said yes and Spearman said no. So the final statement is false.

questions.stem: Which statements about a correlation matrix are TRUE?

options.a: The matrix is symmetric, so r_xy equals r_yx.
options.b: The diagonal is always 1 because each variable is perfectly correlated with itself.
options.c: The strongest association in the states matrix is between income and high-school graduates.
options.d: The strongest association in the states matrix is between murder and frost.
options.e: A correlation matrix can be computed in R with `select(...) |> cor() |> round(2)`.

questions.explanation: Reading the matrix, the largest off-diagonal value in absolute terms is 0.78 between murder and life expectancy, so both (c) and (d) are wrong.
questions.code:
states |>
  select(income, hs_grad, illiteracy, life_exp, murder, frost) |>
  cor() |> round(2)

questions.stem: What is the F-statistic in a one-way ANOVA?

options.a: The ratio of the variance between groups to the variance within groups
options.b: The ratio of the variance within groups to the variance between groups
options.c: The difference between the largest and smallest group means
options.d: The total number of observations divided by the number of groups
options.e: The ratio of the between-group mean square to the overall mean

questions.explanation: F is between-group variance over within-group variance. A large F means the group means differ a lot relative to the noise inside the groups, so the formula is definitely not the reverse as in (b).

questions.stem: Which statements about ANOVA are TRUE?

options.a: ANOVA compares means across multiple groups.
options.b: The null hypothesis is that all group means are equal.
options.c: The alternative is that at least one group mean differs.
options.d: Rejecting H0 tells you which specific groups differ.
options.e: ANOVA with only two groups gives exactly the same p-value as the two-sample t-test with equal variances.

questions.explanation: ANOVA is an omnibus test: rejecting H0 only says something differs, not what. Identifying the differing pairs needs post-hoc tests such as `pairwise.t.test()`, which the lecture mentions but does not cover, so (d) is false.
questions.code: oneway.test(height ~ city, data = heights, var.equal = TRUE)

questions.stem: The lecture notes that for alpha = 0.05 and m = 190 separate tests, the probability of at least one Type I error is about 99.3%. What is the consequence for practice?

options.a: Each individual test should be run at a much smaller alpha.
options.b: We should use omnibus tests that make a single decision for all groups at once.
options.c: The probability of at least one Type I error is bounded by 0.05.
options.d: More tests automatically increase the power of each test.
options.e: Type II errors disappear when many tests are performed.

questions.explanation: Because repeated separate decisions accumulate false positives, the solution is a single omnibus test such as ANOVA, which controls the overall Type I error rate. Merely shrinking alpha for each test wastes power and does not fix the underlying problem of repeated decisions.

questions.stem: Which statements are TRUE?

options.a: The chi-squared statistic compares observed counts to expected counts.
options.b: A goodness-of-fit test checks whether one variable matches an expected distribution.
options.c: A test for homogeneity checks whether a distribution is the same across groups.
options.d: A test for independence checks whether two categorical variables are associated.
options.e: The goodness-of-fit degrees of freedom is k, where k is the number of categories.

questions.explanation: For a goodness-of-fit test the degrees of freedom are k - 1, because one parameter is used up fitting the total, so (e) is false.

questions.stem: Consider this R output. Which statements about it are true?

options.a: X-squared = 1
options.b: df = 5
options.c: p-value = 0.9626
options.d: The test provides evidence that the die is unfair
options.e: The expected count for each face is 10

questions.explanation: Every option here is true. R reports X-squared = 1, df = 5 and p-value = 0.9626, the die has 60 rolls over 6 faces so each expected count is 10, and a p-value of 0.96 is high, meaning we FAIL to reject the fair-die hypothesis - so there is no evidence the die is unfair. Remember that on the real exam a question like this scores the full point if you mark nothing.

questions.stem: Consider this ANOVA output from `oneway.test()`. Which statements about it are true?

options.b: num df = 2 and denom df = 297
options.c: p-value = 1.673e-06
options.d: We accept the null hypothesis that all city means are equal
options.e: There is significant evidence that average height differs between the cities

questions.explanation: Every option here is true. R reports F = 13.915 with numerator df 2 and denominator df 297 and a p-value of 1.673e-06, and such a small p-value means we REJECT H0, so the cities do differ significantly in mean height. Option (d) states the opposite of what the output implies. Mark nothing here to score the full point.
questions.code: oneway.test(height ~ city, data = heights, var.equal = TRUE)

questions.stem: Which statements about the following correlation output are true? `t = 5.4738, df = 48, p-value = 1.579e-06, cor = 0.6199323`.

options.a: The test statistic is 5.4738
options.b: The degrees of freedom are 48
options.c: The sample correlation is 0.6199323
options.d: We fail to reject H0 because the p-value is large
options.e: The data provide evidence of a positive correlation

questions.explanation: Every option here is true. The output reports t = 5.4738, df = 48, p = 1.579e-06 and cor = 0.6199, and because that p-value is far below any usual significance level we REJECT H0 and conclude there is a positive correlation. Option (d) says the opposite. Leaving everything unmarked scores the full point.

questions.stem: Explain what the correlation coefficient measures, and give one situation where a correlation near zero would be misleading.
questions.answer: Correlation measures the strength and direction of the LINEAR association between two continuous variables, running from -1 through 0 to 1. A value near zero only rules out a linear relationship, so it can be misleading when the true pattern is curved or driven by an outlier, as in the states example where Alaska alone produces a moderate Pearson r but almost no Spearman correlation.

rubric.text: Defined as the strength and direction of LINEAR association
Notes zero rules out only a linear relationship
Gives a valid non-linear or outlier example

questions.stem: Explain what the F-statistic in a one-way ANOVA is, what a large value means, and what rejecting the null hypothesis does NOT tell you.
questions.answer: The F-statistic is the ratio of the variance between groups to the variance within groups, and it follows an F distribution with degrees of freedom determined by the number of groups and the sample size. A large F means the group means differ substantially relative to the noise inside the groups. Rejecting H0 only shows that at least one group differs; it does not reveal which groups, which requires post-hoc tests such as `pairwise.t.test()`.

rubric.text: F defined as between-group variance over within-group variance
Explains what a large F indicates
Notes the F distribution and its degrees of freedom
States rejection does not identify which groups differ

questions.stem: Name the three main types of chi-squared test and state the degrees of freedom for a goodness-of-fit test with k categories.
questions.answer: The three types are the goodness-of-fit test, which checks whether one variable matches an expected distribution, the test for homogeneity, which checks whether a distribution is the same across different populations or groups, and the test for independence, which checks whether two categorical variables are associated. For a goodness-of-fit test the degrees of freedom are k - 1, so for a die with k = 6 faces we get df = 5.

rubric.text: All three test types named with correct purpose
Degrees of freedom given as k - 1 with the die example giving 5

questions.topic: Working in R for a chi-squared test
questions.stem: Write the R code for a goodness-of-fit test of a fair die, given observed counts of 8, 10, 9, 12, 11 and 10 over 60 rolls.
questions.answer:
```r
observed <- c(8, 10, 9, 12, 11, 10)
chisq.test(observed, p = rep(1/6, 6))
```
`chisq.test()` with a vector of expected probabilities performs the goodness-of-fit test; the output is X-squared = 1, df = 5, p-value = 0.9626. Since the p-value is very high we fail to reject H0 and find no evidence the die is unfair.

rubric.text: `chisq.test()` used with the observed counts
Expected probabilities given as `rep(1/6, 6)`
Reports the correct output and conclusion

questions.stem: Explain two properties a correlation matrix always has, and describe how you would compute one in R for a data.frame with many numeric variables.
questions.answer: A correlation matrix is symmetric, because r_xy equals r_yx, and its diagonal is always 1, since each variable is perfectly correlated with itself. In R you select the numeric columns of interest and pipe into `cor()`, typically rounding for readability, for example `states |> select(income, hs_grad) |> cor() |> round(2)`, and then read off the strongest off-diagonal entries.

rubric.text: Symmetry correctly identified and justified
Diagonal of 1 correctly identified and justified
R pipeline with select, cor and round given correctly

questions.stem: For each scenario, name the appropriate test: comparing average height across three cities; whether smoking is independent of eye colour; whether a die is fair; and whether two continuous variables move together.
questions.answer: Comparing a mean across three cities uses a one-way ANOVA, for example `oneway.test()`. Whether smoking is independent of eye colour is a chi-squared test for independence. Whether a die is fair is a chi-squared goodness-of-fit test. And whether two continuous variables move together is tested with Pearson correlation via `cor.test()`, or Spearman if the association is non-linear or there are outliers.

rubric.text: ANOVA correctly matched to comparing three city means
Chi-squared independence correctly matched to smoking and eye colour
Chi-squared goodness-of-fit correctly matched to the fair die
Correlation correctly matched to two continuous variables

questions.stem: All the tests seen so far rely on a known sampling distribution such as z, t, F or chi-squared. What is the non-parametric alternative discussed in this lecture?

options.a: Bootstrapping
options.b: The bootstrap permutation test
options.c: Bagging
options.d: Cross-validation
options.e: The jackknife confidence interval

questions.explanation: The lecture defines non-parametric methods as those not assuming a specific form for the population distribution, and states that it focuses on bootstrapping as the workable option, estimating standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values directly from the sample.

questions.stem: What are the steps of a Monte-Carlo simulation as given in the lecture?

options.a: Collect real data, fit a model, test, report
options.b: Define the data generating process and statistic, generate many random samples, compute the statistic for each
options.c: Simulate one sample, plot it, conclude
options.d: Choose alpha, compute the p-value, decide
options.e: Generate samples, bootstrap them, report a confidence interval

questions.explanation: The three steps are to define the DGP and the statistic of interest, generate a large number of random samples from that DGP, and calculate the statistic for each sample so the resulting distribution approximates the sampling distribution.

questions.stem: What does a Monte-Carlo simulation rely on to become accurate?

options.a: The central limit theorem
options.b: The law of large numbers
options.c: The fact that R is fast
options.d: The chi-squared approximation
options.e: Having an exactly normal population

questions.explanation: Monte-Carlo works by repeated sampling, so its accuracy improves as the number of simulations grows, which is precisely the law of large numbers. The CLT is about the shape of a sampling distribution, a different statement.

questions.stem: Consider this R code. What does `H` end up counting?

options.a: The number of simulated draws where X is less than Y
options.b: The number of simulated draws where X is greater than Y
options.c: The sum of X across all simulations
options.d: The number of simulations, N
options.e: The mean of X

questions.explanation: `H <- sum(X < Y)` counts the cases where the comparison is true, so dividing H by N gives the simulated probability P(X < Y). The lecture uses exactly this to estimate a probability that is analytically awkward, here for X normal and Y exponential.
questions.code:
X <- rnorm(N, mean = 3, sd = 1)
Y <- rexp(N, rate = 0.5)
H <- sum(X < Y)
H / N

questions.stem: What does the bootstrapping procedure do?

options.a: It resamples from the fitted normal distribution
options.b: It repeatedly resamples the observed data with replacement to estimate standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values
options.c: It splits the data into a training and a test set
options.d: It computes the exact analytic solution
options.e: It removes outliers before analysing the data

questions.explanation: Bootstrapping samples repeatedly from the empirical distribution of the observed data with replacement and recomputes the statistic each time, giving an estimated sampling distribution without assuming a parametric form.
questions.code:
boot_sample <- sample(x, length(x), replace = TRUE)
boot_medians[i] <- median(boot_sample)

questions.stem: Why is `set.seed()` used before a simulation?

options.a: It makes the simulation run faster
options.b: It makes the random numbers reproducible so results can be recovered
options.c: It increases the number of simulations
options.d: It ensures the data are normally distributed
options.e: It removes the need for a bootstrap

questions.explanation: `set.seed()` fixes the starting state of the random number generator, so the same seed reproduces the same pseudo-random draws. That is essential when a result needs to be reported or checked by someone else.

questions.stem: Consider this code. What is the purpose of `numeric(N)`?

options.a: To create N random numbers
options.b: To create an empty numeric vector of length N that will hold one bootstrap statistic per iteration
options.c: To create a vector of N observations to resample
options.d: To pre-allocate a data.frame with N rows
options.e: To set the random seed N times

questions.explanation: `numeric(N)` allocates an empty numeric vector of length N so R can store one bootstrap result in each position. Without pre-allocation R would have to grow the vector inside the loop, which is slower.

questions.stem: Consider this code. Which statements about it are true?

options.a: `N <- 100000` sets the number of simulations
options.b: `X <- rnorm(N, mean = 3, sd = 1)` draws N values from a normal distribution
options.c: `H <- sum(X < Y)` counts the draws where X is less than Y
options.d: `H / N` gives an estimate of P(X < Y)
options.e: The result is the exact analytical probability of P(X < Y)

questions.explanation: Every option here is true. The code sets the simulation count, draws from the two distributions, counts the favourable cases and divides by N to estimate P(X < Y). The final option overstates it: this is a simulation-based approximation, accurate as N grows by the law of large numbers, not an exact closed-form answer. Mark nothing to score the full point.
questions.code:
N <- 100000
X <- rnorm(N, mean = 3, sd = 1)
Y <- rexp(N, rate = 0.5)
H <- sum(X < Y)
H / N

questions.stem: Which statements about the birthday problem simulation are true?

options.a: `sample(1:365, 30, replace = TRUE)` simulates 30 people's birthdays
options.b: The replacement is appropriate because two people can share a birthday
options.c: The simulation estimates the probability of at least one shared birthday
options.d: The simulation would be exact regardless of how large N is
options.e: Increasing N generally improves the accuracy of the estimate

questions.explanation: Every option here is true. Sampling 30 birthdays with replacement from 1 to 365 models independent birthdays, repeating it estimates the probability of a shared birthday, and raising N improves accuracy through the law of large numbers. The fourth option is wrong: no finite N gives an exact answer. Mark nothing to score the full point.

questions.stem: Explain what Monte-Carlo simulation is, list its three steps, and say which theoretical result it relies on.
questions.answer: A Monte-Carlo simulation generates a large number of random samples from a specified data generating process to approximate the sampling distribution of a statistic, which is useful for standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values when analytic solutions are difficult. The steps are to define the data generating process and the statistic of interest, generate a large number of random samples, and calculate the statistic for each sample. It relies on the law of large numbers, since the approximation improves as the number of simulations grows.

rubric.text: Defined as approximating a sampling distribution by repeated sampling
All three steps listed
Law of large numbers correctly named as the basis
Notes use for standard errors, CIs or p-values when analytics are hard

questions.stem: Assume X is normal with mean 3 and standard deviation 1, and Y is exponential with rate 0.5. Describe how you would use a simulation to estimate P(X < Y), writing the relevant R code.
questions.answer: Generate N values from each distribution, count how often the comparison holds, and divide by N. In R: `X <- rnorm(N, mean = 3, sd = 1)`, `Y <- rexp(N, rate = 0.5)`, `H <- sum(X < Y)`, then `H / N` is the estimated probability, which for large N settles near 0.25. The analytic solution is awkward, which is exactly the case simulation is meant for.

rubric.text: Both distributions generated with `rnorm()` and `rexp()` and correct parameters
Count of favourable cases computed with `sum(X < Y)`
Estimate obtained as the count divided by N

questions.code:
X <- rnorm(N, mean = 3, sd = 1)
Y <- rexp(N, rate = 0.5)
H <- sum(X < Y)
H / N

questions.stem: Explain how you would bootstrap a median, writing the R code, and say why you cannot simply do this with a mean on the exam.
questions.answer: Resample the observed data with replacement many times, compute the median of each resample, and use the distribution of those medians to form a confidence interval. In R: pre-allocate with `boot_medians <- numeric(N)`, then in a loop over `i in 1:N` take `boot_sample <- sample(x, length(x), replace = TRUE)` and store `boot_medians[i] <- median(boot_sample)`. The bootstrap is an approximation that improves with N, not an exact calculation, so you describe the procedure rather than compute a number.

rubric.text: Resampling with replacement correctly described
Median computed for each resample and stored
R code given including pre-allocation with `numeric(N)`
Notes the bootstrap approximates rather than computes exactly

questions.stem: Explain what a non-parametric method is, and why simulation-based inference is needed at all given that we already have z, t, F and chi-squared tests.
questions.answer: A non-parametric method makes no assumption about the specific form of the population distribution, unlike the parametric tests that rely on a known sampling distribution justified by normality or the central limit theorem. Simulation is needed because when the normality assumption is violated, especially with small samples, the standard tests can give unreliable results, and sometimes the mathematics of the analytic solution is simply too hard.

rubric.text: Defined as making no assumption about the population distribution form
Contrasts with the parametric tests relying on known sampling distributions
Notes unreliability when normality is violated, especially at small n
Notes analytic solutions can be too difficult to obtain

questions.stem: Explain the purpose of `set.seed()` and describe what happens to your simulated results if you do not use it.
questions.answer: `set.seed()` fixes the initial state of R's random number generator, so the same seed always produces the same sequence of pseudo-random draws. Without it, each run starts from a different state, so a Monte-Carlo or bootstrap result will differ slightly every time you run it, which makes results impossible to reproduce, report or have checked by someone else.

rubric.text: Explains it fixes the random number generator state
States that the same seed reproduces the same draws
Explains results differ between runs without it

questions.stem: The lecture checks a probability analytically and then suggests simulating it. Give the analytic approach and the simulation approach for the probability of obtaining 1, 5 or 9 heads in 10 tosses of a fair coin.
questions.answer: Analytically, the number of heads in 10 tosses follows a binomial distribution with n = 10 and p = 0.5, so the probability is P(X = 1) + P(X = 5) + P(X = 9), which evaluates to about 0.2656. The simulation approach instead draws many samples of 10 coin tosses, counts the fraction of samples with 1, 5 or 9 heads, and uses that fraction as an estimate that converges on the analytic value as N grows.

rubric.text: Identifies the binomial distribution with n = 10 and p = 0.5
Correctly sums P(X=1), P(X=5) and P(X=9) and gives about 0.2656
Describes the simulation as repeated draws with a sample fraction
Notes convergence to the analytic value as N grows

questions.stem: Describe how the birthday problem would be simulated in R, and explain why the sampling is done with replacement.
questions.answer: Draw 30 birthdays at random from the 365 possible days with `sample(1:365, 30, replace = TRUE)`, check whether any day repeats within that draw, and record whether a match occurred. Repeat this for a large number of iterations and divide the number of iterations with a match by the total to estimate the probability. Replacement is correct because different people are independent, so two of them really can share a birthday; sampling without replacement would make a shared birthday impossible.

rubric.text: 30 birthdays drawn from 1 to 365
Describes detecting a repeated day and averaging over iterations
Justifies replacement by independence of different people
Notes without replacement a match would be impossible

questions.answer: This lecture adds simulation-based inference: Monte-Carlo simulation to approximate sampling distributions and awkward probabilities, and bootstrapping to estimate standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values without assuming a parametric form. Linear regression, along with a fuller treatment of correlation, is explicitly deferred to the next course in the programme, SDS2.

rubric.text: Identifies Monte-Carlo simulation as the addition
Identifies bootstrapping as the second addition
Correctly defers linear regression to SDS2
